title: Peripheral Neuropathy
subject: Medicine
summary: Peripheral neuropathy is damage to peripheral nerves causing sensory, motor and autonomic deficits. Diagnosis relies on history, focused exam and targeted investigations, especially where resources are limited.

sections.p: Peripheral neuropathy refers to dysfunction of peripheral nerves beyond the spinal cord, presenting with sensory loss, pain, weakness or autonomic change. Diagnosis requires a compatible clinical picture and exclusion of mimics.
b: Distinguish distal symmetric polyneuropathy from mononeuritis multiplex.
Identify length‑dependent pattern (feet before hands).

sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom burden and functional impact, often using the Toronto Clinical Scoring System (0‑19). Staging guides urgency of treatment.
b: Mild: score ≤5, minimal functional loss.
Moderate: score 6‑12, gait disturbance or daily activity limitation.
Severe: score >12, profound weakness or autonomic failure.

sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings, the most common etiologies are infectious, metabolic and drug‑related.
b: Diabetes mellitus – leading cause worldwide.
HIV infection and antiretroviral neurotoxicity.
Isoniazid therapy – pyridoxine deficiency.
Alcohol excess – nutritional deficiency.
Malaria or schistosomiasis‑related vasculitis (rare).
Herbal remedies containing neurotoxic compounds.

sections.p: Patients usually report a gradual, symmetric numbness and tingling that starts in the toes and ascends. Pain may be burning or electric. Weakness, foot drop, and autonomic signs (dry skin, orthostatic hypotension) can appear later.
b: Positive sensory symptoms (paresthesia, dysesthesia).
Loss of vibration and pin‑prick in a stocking‑glove distribution.
Reduced ankle reflexes early; later may involve knee reflexes.
Motor weakness progressing proximally.

sections.p: When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical clues (e.g., diabetic history, HIV risk factors) and treat empirically while arranging referral.

t.b: Is diabetes present? – Elevated glucose/HbA1c confirms diabetic neuropathy.
Is HIV infection a cause? – Positive test prompts ART review.
Is B12 deficiency contributing? – Low level suggests pernicious or dietary cause.

t.a: Serum folate & methylmalonic acid (if B12 unavailable)
t.b: Distinguish folate from B12 deficiency – Normal MMA with low folate points to folate deficiency.
Characterise axonal vs demyelinating pattern – Guides prognosis and specific causes.
Screen for diabetic nephropathy as a systemic complication – Proteinuria indicates renal involvement.

sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent action.
b: Rapidly progressive weakness or respiratory involvement.
Severe autonomic dysfunction (e.g., orthostatic collapse).
Unexplained weight loss or fever suggesting vasculitis.
New onset foot ulceration due to loss of protective sensation.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide symptomatic and supportive care.
b: Glycaemic control for diabetes – tight control slows progression.
Antiretroviral regimen review if neurotoxic agents present.
Analgesia: gabapentin or pregabalin (first‑line) for neuropathic pain; avoid high‑dose opioids.
Foot care education and protective footwear to prevent ulcers.
Physiotherapy to maintain strength and gait.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of symptom score, glycaemic status and drug toxicities is essential.
b: Re‑assess Toronto score every 3‑6 months.
Screen for diabetic retinopathy and nephropathy concurrently.
Encourage abstinence from alcohol and safe use of herbal medicines.
Peripheral vascular disease – causes claudication without sensory loss.
Myopathy – presents with proximal weakness but preserved sensation.
Radiculopathy – dermatomal distribution rather than stocking‑glove.
Normal B12 level does not exclude functional deficiency; check MMA if suspicion remains.
Negative HIV rapid test in early infection – repeat after window period if risk persists.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of ability to walk or breathe
Rapidly spreading skin lesions suggesting vasculitis

faq.a: It depletes pyridoxine, a co‑factor for neurotransmitter synthesis, leading to nerve damage.
If the underlying cause is identified and treated early, symptoms may improve; chronic damage may be permanent.

faq.q: What is the first step when a patient presents with new peripheral neuropathy?
faq.a: Take a focused history for diabetes, HIV, drug exposure and nutritional deficiencies, then perform a targeted neurological exam.

exam: What bedside tests would you perform to differentiate a length‑dependent polyneuropathy from a mononeuritis multiplex? — Test vibration, pin‑prick, reflexes in a stocking‑glove pattern; look for asymmetric focal deficits.

How does HIV‑related neuropathy differ clinically from diabetic neuropathy? — HIV neuropathy often has a distal symmetric pattern with prominent pain and may occur at younger age without hyperglycaemia.

A patient presents with foot ulceration and loss of sensation. Which red flag does this represent and what is the immediate action? — Loss of protective sensation is a complication; arrange wound care, off‑loading and urgent podiatry review.
Explain why a normal serum B12 does not completely rule out B12‑related neuropathy. — Functional deficiency can exist; elevated methylmalonic acid would confirm true deficiency.
When nerve conduction studies are unavailable, how can you still stage severity? — Use clinical scoring systems (Toronto) and functional assessment of gait and activities of daily living.
Why are opioids generally avoided as first‑line therapy for neuropathic pain? — They provide limited benefit for neuropathic mechanisms and carry high risk of dependence and side‑effects.
What autonomic signs would alert you to a life‑threatening complication of neuropathy? — Orthostatic hypotension, severe constipation, urinary retention, or cardiac arrhythmias.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam differentiate length‑dependent polyneuropathy from mononeuritis multiplex and reveal red‑flag features.
b: Onset: gradual vs acute; months‑long suggests metabolic, days‑weeks suggests vasculitis or toxin
Symmetry: stocking‑glove distribution points to polyneuropathy; focal deficits suggest mononeuritis
Risk factors: diabetes, HIV, TB treatment, alcohol, malnutrition, chemotherapy, herbal remedies
Pain quality: burning/dysesthetic vs sharp lancinating
Autonomic symptoms: orthostatic dizziness, gastroparesis, urinary retention, erectile dysfunction
Functional impact: gait instability, falls, need for assistive devices
Systemic red flags: fever, weight loss, rapid weakness, respiratory muscle involvement

t.b: Look for foot ulceration, deformities, muscle wasting; positive indicates chronic motor neuropathy or loss of protective sensation
Use 10‑g monofilament, tuning fork (128 Hz) and pin‑prick; loss of vibration or pin‑prick in a stocking pattern confirms length‑dependent loss; bedside test cannot quantify axonal loss
Tap ankle then knee; absent ankle reflex early in polyneuropathy; preserved reflexes suggest central or focal process
Medical Research Council grading of foot dorsiflexors and plantar flexors; weakness indicates motor fiber involvement; bedside cannot differentiate demyelination vs axonal loss
Measure supine and standing BP/HR; orthostatic drop >20 mmHg systolic or >10 mmHg diastolic signals autonomic failure; bedside cannot grade severity of sudomotor loss

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; interpret results with local reference ranges and consider alternatives when unavailable.
b: Full blood count – screens for anemia, infection, eosinophilia (vasculitis)
Fasting glucose/HbA1c – confirms diabetic etiology; HbA1c ≥7 % supports chronic hyperglycaemia
Serum B12 and MMA – normal B12 does not exclude functional deficiency; elevated MMA confirms B12‑related neuropathy
HIV ELISA/viral load – positive result directs to HIV‑associated distal sensory polyneuropathy

t.b: Answers: demyelinating vs axonal pattern; reduced amplitude with normal velocity = axonal loss typical of diabetic neuropathy; unavailable → rely on clinical severity scores
Detects denervation in distal muscles; fibrillation potentials support axonal neuropathy; if unavailable, monitor motor weakness progression
Identifies renal failure causing uremic neuropathy; eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m² raises suspicion
Elevated transaminases may indicate alcoholic or drug‑induced neuropathy; normal LFT does not exclude nutritional deficiency
Detects lead or arsenic exposure; positive result mandates chelation; if unavailable, obtain exposure history

sections.p: Apply recognised criteria to classify neuropathy and guide management decisions.
b: Diagnosis requires compatible history, length‑dependent sensory loss, and at least one objective sign (reflex loss, abnormal NCS, or monofilament deficit)
Toronto Clinical Scoring System: 0‑5 mild, 6‑12 moderate, >12 severe; score based on symptoms, sensory loss, reflexes, and motor function
Severity grading incorporates functional impact: mild – no gait change; moderate – gait instability or activity limitation; severe – wheelchair dependence, autonomic crisis, or ulceration
Stage 1 (early) – sensory symptoms only; Stage 2 – sensory plus reflex loss; Stage 3 – motor weakness appears; Stage 4 – autonomic failure or complications

sections.p: Conditions that mimic peripheral neuropathy must be considered, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Mononeuritis multiplex – painful, asymmetric deficits; nerve biopsy or angiography separates from polyneuropathy
Radiculopathy – dermatomal sensory loss with back pain; straight‑leg raise and MRI differentiate
Myopathy – proximal weakness without sensory loss; CK elevation and EMG pattern distinguish
Peripheral vascular disease – claudication pain, preserved sensation; ankle‑brachial index <0.9 confirms vascular cause

t.b: Points: acute painful focal deficits, systemic vasculitis signs; separate by lack of stocking‑glove pattern and presence of multiple nerve territories
Points: back pain, dermatomal distribution, positive straight‑leg raise; MRI or CT confirms nerve root compression
Points: absent pulses, cool skin, ulcer with poor healing; ankle‑brachial index <0.9 differentiates from pure neuropathy

sections.p: Treat neuropathy in a staged, resource‑aware manner, prioritising reversible causes, pain control, and functional recovery.
b: 1. Identify and treat reversible cause (e.g., stop neurotoxic drugs, give pyridoxine for isoniazid, correct vitamin B12 deficiency).
2. Initiate first‑line neuropathic pain therapy (gabapentinoids or duloxetine) unless contraindicated.
3. Provide non‑pharmacologic support (exercise, balance training, footwear, foot care education).
4. Monitor symptom progression with a simple clinical score (Toronto Clinical Scoring System) every 4–6 weeks.
5. Escalate to stronger analgesics (opioids) only if pain is uncontrolled and other measures fail, monitoring for sedation and constipation.
6. Refer to specialist or tertiary centre if rapid progression, respiratory weakness, severe autonomic instability, or if investigations are inconclusive.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Neuropathic agents and treatments carry specific adverse effects and interactions that must be anticipated and managed.
b: Gabapentinoids: sedation, dizziness, weight gain – counsel patients to avoid driving until effect known; monitor for worsening depression.
Duloxetine: nausea, dry mouth, increased blood pressure – check baseline BP, avoid in severe hypertension.
Opioids: constipation, respiratory depression, delirium – prescribe laxatives, educate on safe use, avoid in severe COPD.
Antiretroviral neurotoxicity (e.g., stavudine): monitor for neuropathic symptoms, consider regimen change if severe.
Chemotherapy agents (vincristine, cisplatin): monitor for neuropathy, dose‑adjust or switch if cumulative dose limits reached.

sections.p: Neuropathy can lead to serious complications; early recognition dictates escalation of care.
b: Foot ulceration or infection – refer to wound care team, start antibiotics if signs of infection.
Severe autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic hypotension, cardiac arrhythmia) – urgent cardiology or ICU referral.
Rapidly progressive weakness or respiratory compromise – immediate neurology and possible ventilatory support.
Unexplained weight loss or fever – evaluate for vasculitic or infectious causes, consider biopsy.

sections.p: Multiple comorbidities alter presentation, investigations and treatment choices.
b: HIV: increases risk of sensory neuropathy, may mask diabetic neuropathy; use antiretroviral regimens with lower neurotoxicity.
Malnutrition: low protein and vitamin levels worsen neuropathy; provide balanced diet and supplements.
Pregnancy: avoid teratogenic drugs (e.g., duloxetine), use gabapentinoids cautiously.
Diabetes: high glucose worsens neuropathy; tight glycaemic control is essential.
Herbal remedies: some contain neurotoxins; inquire about use.
Alcohol: chronic intake exacerbates neuropathy; advise cessation.
Renal failure: dose‑adjust gabapentinoids and duloxetine; avoid nephrotoxic agents.
Liver failure: limit duloxetine, monitor for hepatotoxicity.
Age extremes: elderly may have atypical presentation, increased sensitivity to opioids; children require lower doses and careful monitoring.

sections.p: Tailor assessment and management to the unique needs of vulnerable populations.
b: Children: use age‑appropriate pain scales, avoid high‑dose opioids, prefer gabapentinoids.
Pregnancy: avoid teratogenic drugs, use lowest effective dose of gabapentinoids, monitor fetal growth.
Elderly: start low, go slow with analgesics, monitor for falls and cognitive changes.
People with HIV: prioritize antiretroviral regimens with minimal neurotoxicity, monitor for drug interactions.
Low‑resource settings: rely on clinical scoring, use inexpensive drugs (gabapentin, amitriptyline), provide education on foot care, and use community health workers for follow‑up.

facts: Toronto Clinical Scoring System: 0‑5 mild, 6‑12 moderate, >12 severe
Length‑dependent neuropathy: symptoms start in toes then ascend to fingers
Distal symmetric polyneuropathy vs mononeuritis multiplex: stocking‑glove loss vs patchy nerve distribution
Common drug‑induced causes: stavudine, vincristine, taxanes, platinum agents
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy most common presentation in men: erectile dysfunction
Nerve conduction: reduced amplitude = axonal loss; velocity normal = demyelination absent
Alcoholic neuropathy: thiamine deficiency, symmetric distal sensory loss
HIV neuropathy: distal painful sensory neuropathy, often with normal nerve studies
Red flag: rapid progression, respiratory muscle weakness, autonomic collapse

vivas.q: What bedside tests differentiate distal symmetric polyneuropathy from mononeuritis multiplex?
vivas.a: Perform vibration/pin‑prick testing in a stocking‑glove pattern, compare reflexes, and test individual nerve territories (e.g., ulnar, radial) for focal deficits.

vivas.q: How does HIV‑related neuropathy differ clinically from diabetic neuropathy?
vivas.a: HIV neuropathy is often painful, distal, and may occur with normal glucose; diabetic neuropathy is more associated with sensory loss and autonomic signs.

vivas.q: Which vitamin must be supplemented with high‑dose isoniazid to prevent neuropathy?
Which class of plant‑derived antineoplastic drugs causes neuropathy by disrupting microtubule assembly?
What specific foot change is caused by motor neuropathy in diabetic foot disease?
vivas.a: Intrinsic muscle wasting leading to claw toe and hammer toe deformities.

vivas.q: Primary pathological mechanism of tri‑cresyl phosphate‑induced neuropathy?
vivas.a: Organophosphate‑induced axonal degeneration of distal motor neurons.

vivas.q: Which vinca alkaloid is dose‑limited by peripheral neuropathy rather than myelosuppression?
Name a plant alkaloid commonly causing chemotherapy‑induced peripheral neuropathy.
Nerve study shows reduced amplitude, normal velocity. What pathology does this suggest?
vivas.a: Predominant axonal loss with preserved myelin.

vivas.q: Most common autonomic presentation in male diabetics?
vivas.a: Erectile dysfunction due to parasympathetic loss.

vivas.q: Why are opioids avoided as first‑line therapy for neuropathic pain?
vivas.a: They provide limited relief, risk dependence, and worsen constipation which can exacerbate neuropathy complications.

vivas.q: What urgent red flag does foot ulceration with loss of sensation represent?
vivas.a: Impending infection and possible osteomyelitis requiring immediate debridement and antibiotics.

vivas.q: How would you stage severity when nerve conduction studies are unavailable?
vivas.a: Use the Toronto Clinical Scoring System based on symptom burden and functional impact.

vivas.q: What bedside sign cannot differentiate axonal from demyelinating neuropathy?
vivas.a: Absent reflexes; both patterns can produce it.

vivas.q: When a patient on antiretroviral therapy presents with painful stocking‑glove neuropathy, what is the next step?
vivas.a: Assess for stavudine or didanosine use and consider switching regimen; add gabapentin or duloxetine for pain control.

vivas.q: What is the first‑line pharmacologic treatment for diabetic peripheral neuropathic pain?
vivas.a: Duloxetine or pregabalin, titrated to effect.

vivas.q: Which investigation confirms B12‑related neuropathy when serum B12 is normal?
vivas.a: Measure methylmalonic acid or homocysteine – elevated levels indicate functional B12 deficiency.

vivas.q: How do you assess autonomic dysfunction at the bedside?
vivas.a: Check orthostatic blood pressure, heart rate variability, resting tachycardia, and inquire about gastrointestinal motility and bladder function.

mcqs.q: A 55‑year‑old diabetic man presents with burning feet, loss of vibration sense, and absent ankle reflexes. Which drug is most appropriate as first‑line analgesic?
mcqs.e: Duloxetine is first‑line for diabetic neuropathic pain.

mcqs.q: A patient on high‑dose isoniazid develops peripheral neuropathy. Which supplement prevents this?
mcqs.e: Isoniazid antagonises vitamin B6, requiring pyridoxine supplementation.

mcqs.q: Which finding distinguishes mononeuritis multiplex from distal symmetric polyneuropathy?
o: Patchy focal deficits in separate nerves
mcqs.e: Mononeuritis multiplex shows asymmetric, focal nerve involvement.

mcqs.q: A cancer patient on vincristine develops severe peripheral neuropathy. Which symptom is most typical?
mcqs.e: Vincristine causes motor neuropathy leading to foot drop.

mcqs.q: In nerve conduction studies of diabetic neuropathy, amplitude is reduced while velocity is near normal. This pattern indicates:
mcqs.e: Reduced amplitude with preserved velocity reflects axonal degeneration.

mcqs.q: Which autonomic symptom is most common in male diabetics?
mcqs.e: Erectile dysfunction is the prevalent autonomic manifestation in men.

cases.v: 45‑year‑old man with type 2 diabetes presents with burning toes, loss of ankle reflexes, and a 1‑cm ulcer on the plantar surface of the right foot. No fever. Vibration sense absent to the mid‑shin.

qs.q: Which bedside test confirms autonomic involvement?
qs.a: Measure orthostatic blood pressure; a drop ≥20 mmHg systolic indicates autonomic dysfunction.

qs.q: Initial management steps for his neuropathy and ulcer?
qs.a: Optimize glycaemic control, start duloxetine for pain, provide pyridoxine if on isoniazid, off‑load ulcer with a total contact cast, and start broad‑spectrum antibiotics if infection suspected.

cases.v: 30‑year‑old woman with newly diagnosed HIV, CD4 250, on stavudine‑based ART, complains of painful tingling in both feet worsening over months. Examination shows reduced pin‑prick, normal reflexes, no motor weakness.

qs.q: What is the most likely cause of her neuropathy?
qs.a: Stavudine‑induced distal sensory neuropathy, a toxic effect of nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors.

qs.q: What investigation would you order if nerve studies are unavailable?
qs.a: Use the Toronto Clinical Scoring System based on symptoms and functional impact to stage severity.

qs.q: Management plan for her neuropathic pain?
qs.a: Switch to a less neurotoxic ART regimen if possible, add gabapentin or duloxetine for pain, and ensure pyridoxine supplementation.

mistakes: Prescribing high‑dose opioids as first‑line for neuropathic pain, ignoring limited efficacy and side‑effects
Failing to give pyridoxine with isoniazid, leading to preventable B6 deficiency neuropathy
Confusing B12 deficiency with isoniazid toxicity; isoniazid antagonises B6, not B12
Relying solely on nerve conduction studies to stage severity when they may be unavailable
Missing autonomic signs such as orthostatic hypotension, which are red flags for life‑threatening complications
Assuming all peripheral neuropathies are length‑dependent; mononeuritis multiplex requires a different diagnostic approach
